title: Fault finding
summary: A calm, step-by-step way to work out what is wrong, applied to the faults you are most likely to meet. Use it alongside the Fault finder tab.

lessons.title: A systematic approach
lessons.intro: When an engine misbehaves, it is tempting to start taking things apart. A few minutes spent thinking first usually finds the fault faster, and avoids creating new problems.

diagram.caption: A simple order of work for any engine fault.

labels.title: Make the boat safe
labels.detail: Sail, anchor or get a tow before working on the engine.

labels.title: Gather the clues
labels.detail: What happened, when, and what changed beforehand.

labels.title: Think in systems
labels.detail: Fuel, air, compression, cooling, lubrication, electrics.

labels.title: Change one thing at a time
labels.detail: And check the result after each change.

labels.title: Know when to stop
labels.detail: Get help before a fault becomes damage.

diagram.description: A flow diagram of six steps for fault finding: make the boat safe, gather the clues, think in systems, check the simple things first, change one thing at a time, and know when to stop and get help.

steps.title: The boat comes first
steps.text: A failed engine is rarely an emergency in itself, but losing propulsion near rocks, in a busy channel or in strong tide can be. Deal with the boat's safety first: sail, anchor, or call for help. Then turn to the engine.

steps.title: Gather the clues
steps.text: Note what the engine did and how: a slow fade or a sudden stop, any noise, smoke, smell, warning light or alarm. Ask what changed recently: refuelling, rough weather, a filter change, a new crew member operating the controls.

steps.title: Think in systems
steps.text: To run, a diesel needs clean fuel free of air, clean air, and good compression. To keep running it also needs cooling and lubrication, and to start it needs the electrics and enough heat. Decide which system the clues point to.

steps.title: Simple things first
steps.text: Check the easy causes before the difficult ones: control positions, switches, levels, filters and the strainer, before injectors or internal parts. The Fault finder lists possible causes for each symptom without ranking them, so use your clues to decide where to start.

steps.title: One change at a time
steps.text: Make one change, then test. If you change several things at once, you will not know which one mattered, and you may introduce a new fault.

steps.title: Know when to stop
steps.text: Some conditions mean stop the engine first and do not restart until the cause is found: low oil pressure, overheating, water coming in, suspected water in the engine, fuel spraying, smoke or fire, and an uncontrolled leak at the shaft seal. The Fault finder has a card for each. If you are unsure, get advice from a qualified marine engineer.

lessons.reviewNote: S16 and the Fault finder judgement: the lesson now lists the seven stop conditions that have Fault finder cards, and no longer says the Fault finder ranks causes. Please approve.

lessons.title: When the engine will not start
lessons.intro: Starting failures divide roughly in two. Either the engine does not turn over properly, which usually points to the starting circuit, or it turns over but will not fire, which usually points to the stop control, fuel or heat.
lessons.caution: Crank only in short bursts, as your handbook advises, and keep hands, hair and clothing clear of belts and pulleys.

steps.title: First, the controls
steps.text: Before anything else, check the gear lever is in neutral, the stop control is pushed fully home, and the battery isolator and key switch are on. These catch out experienced skippers too.

steps.title: If it does not turn over
steps.text: Work along the electrical path: battery charge, battery terminals, isolator, fuse or breaker for the panel, the starter solenoid and the engine earth. A click with no turning usually means not enough current is getting through.

steps.title: If it turns but will not fire
steps.text: Check the stop control is fully home and that no engine fault or immobiliser is preventing a start; some electronic engines show a warning. Then check the fuel: tank level, fuel valve open, no water in the filter bowl. If the fuel system has been opened or run dry, it probably needs bleeding (lesson 2.4). Also make sure the air intake is not blocked. A worn engine with low compression can also struggle, especially from cold.

steps.title: Cold weather
steps.text: On a cold day, make sure you have pre-heated for long enough, as the handbook describes. If the engine starts once warm but struggles from cold, suspect the glow plugs or their circuit.

steps.title: Protect the engine while cranking
steps.text: Crank in short bursts with rests between. On an engine with a wet exhaust, follow the waterlock warning at the top of this lesson: if it repeatedly cranks without starting, stop and follow the engine and exhaust maker's procedure rather than carrying on.

steps.title: When to stop trying
steps.text: If the engine turns a little and then stops hard, or you hear water, stop cranking and do not crank again. Water may have entered the cylinders, and forcing the engine round can bend internal parts. Get qualified assistance.

lessons.reviewNote: Audit note 30, safety revise (P0, S01), and S13: the advice to close the seacock during long cranking is removed; warning A is now shown before the steps, verbatim, and any seawater isolation is left to a documented manufacturer procedure. The won't-fire step now covers the stop control, electronic inhibit, fuel, air intake, pre-heating and compression. Please approve.

lessons.title: When the engine stops or loses power
lessons.intro: An engine that stops by itself, or slowly loses power, is usually being starved of fuel or air, or is being overloaded. How it stopped is your best clue.
lessons.caution: Never go near the propeller, in the water or from a dinghy, unless the engine is stopped and cannot be started.

steps.title: A slow fade
steps.text: If the revs drop away over several seconds, or the engine hunts up and down before stopping, think fuel: a blocked filter, water in the fuel, air getting in, a blocked tank vent or an empty tank.

steps.title: A sudden stop when put in gear
steps.text: If the engine stops the moment it is put in gear, or with a thump, something round the propeller is one important possibility; others include an idle speed set too low, a gearbox fault or a binding shaft. Stop the engine and make sure it cannot be started before you inspect anything near the propeller or shaft.

steps.title: A hard stop with a warning
steps.text: If the engine stopped with an alarm, a bang, a burning smell or a jolt, do not restart it. It may have overheated, lost oil pressure or seized.

steps.title: Gradual loss of power
steps.text: If the engine runs but will not reach its usual revs, or the boat is slower at the same revs, look at the air filter, the fuel filters, the exhaust for blockages, and the hull and propeller for fouling.

steps.title: After rough weather
steps.text: Many fuel-related stops happen after a rough passage, when dirt and water are stirred up from the bottom of the tank. Check the primary filter bowl first and change the elements if needed.

steps.title: Getting going again
steps.text: After clearing a fuel problem, bleed the system if air has got in, using the handbook's owner procedure (lesson 2.4). Then run the engine at moderate power for a while and watch it, in case the cause returns.

lessons.reviewNote: S12: stalling in gear is now 'one important possibility', with idle speed, gearbox and shaft binding listed and a safe-inspection instruction. Please approve.

lessons.title: Overheating, smoke and alarms
lessons.intro: Warning lights, alarms and smoke are the engine's way of telling you something is wrong before it fails. Knowing which ones mean stop now, and which mean investigate soon, protects both the engine and the boat.
lessons.caution: Keep clear of hot exhaust parts, belts and pulleys, and let the engine cool before you work on it.

steps.title: Stop now
steps.text: Low oil pressure and overheating are stop-engine conditions: follow the instructions at the top of this lesson. The Fault finder's stop cards list the other conditions that mean stop first.

steps.title: Overheating: use the clues
steps.text: Once the engine has stopped and cooled, start with what you saw. Little or no water from the exhaust points to the raw water side: intake, seacock, strainer, pump drive or impeller. Normal water flow but still overheating points to the belt, coolant level, thermostat or heat exchanger.

steps.title: Reading the smoke
steps.text: White smoke that clears as the engine warms is often unburnt fuel on a cold start. Black smoke under load suggests too much fuel for the air: check the air filter and look for overloading. Blue smoke suggests oil is being burnt. Steam with little exhaust water points to a cooling problem.

steps.title: Charge warning
steps.text: A charge warning is not usually an emergency in itself; it indicates a charging-system fault. Check the belt straight away: if it has broken and also drives the coolant pump, the engine will soon overheat.

steps.title: After the alarm
steps.text: Restart only once the cause has been found and corrected, then watch the gauges and warning lights closely. If the warning comes back, stop again and get advice.

steps.title: False alarms
steps.text: Sensors and wiring can fail, but treat every warning as real until you have proved otherwise. An engine that is damaged because a real warning was ignored costs far more than an unnecessary stop.

lessons.reviewNote: S03 and S04: stop-engine conditions C and D now open the lesson, verbatim; overheating checks happen only after the engine has cooled; 'most overheating starts on the raw water side' is removed; restarting only once the cause is corrected. Please approve.

questions.prompt: Your engine stops while you are motoring near a rocky shore. What should you do first?
options: Make the boat safe: sail, anchor or call for help
Open the engine space and start looking for the fault
Keep trying to start the engine until it runs
Check the fuel filter bowl for water straight away
questions.explanation: The boat's safety comes before the engine. Opening up the engine or cranking it while the boat drifts towards rocks puts everyone in danger. Once you are no longer at risk, you can work on the engine calmly.

questions.prompt: Why is it useful to ask 'what changed recently?' when an engine develops a fault?
options: Recent events, such as refuelling, often point straight to the cause
It tells you which part to replace without any further checks
It is the first question an insurer will ask after a claim
It tells you how old the engine is and when it was built
questions.explanation: A fault that appears after refuelling suggests fuel quality; after a filter change, air or a poor seal. Linking the fault to a recent event narrows the search quickly.

questions.prompt: Which three things does a diesel engine need in order to run?
options: Clean fuel free of air, clean air, and good compression
A charged battery, clean fuel and cooling water
Coolant, a fully charged battery and a full fuel tank
A gearbox, a propeller and a stern gland
questions.explanation: Compression heats the air, the fuel is injected and burns. If any of the three is missing, the engine will not run. Cooling, lubrication and electrics matter too, but for keeping going and starting.

questions.prompt: Why should you change only one thing at a time when fault finding?
options: So you can tell which change fixed the problem, without adding new faults
So the engine does not need bleeding more than once
Because most engine tools are designed to be used one at a time
So the job takes longer and is therefore done more carefully
questions.explanation: If you change several things and the engine runs, you will not know which mattered. Each extra change also adds a chance of a new problem, such as letting air into the fuel.

questions.prompt: In what order should you usually check possible causes?
options: Simple and common causes first, difficult and rare ones later
The most expensive parts first, as they matter most
Whichever parts of the engine are easiest to reach
Internal engine parts first, then the outside ones
questions.explanation: Most faults have simple causes such as a control left in the wrong place, a blocked filter or a closed valve. Checking those first saves time and avoids unnecessary dismantling.

questions.prompt: Your engine stops while you are crossing a busy channel. Which order of actions is best?
options: Make the boat safe, gather the clues, then check the simple causes first
Check the simple causes first, gather the clues, then make the boat safe
Gather the clues, try restarting several times, then make the boat safe
Make the boat safe, then change both fuel filters straight away
questions.explanation: The boat comes first: trying to restart while drifting in a busy channel puts the boat at risk of collision. Once it is safe, note how the engine stopped and what changed, then check the easy causes before dismantling anything or changing parts on a guess.
questions.reviewNote: New in content 1.1 (S20): a safety-first ordering question. Please approve.

questions.prompt: The engine turns over at normal speed but will not fire. Which is a sensible first check?
options: That the stop control is fully home, then the fuel supply
The battery terminals, because a weak battery causes this
The raw water strainer, because a blocked one stops it firing
The starter solenoid, because it may not be engaging fully
questions.explanation: If the engine turns normally, the battery and starter are doing their job. Sensible first checks are the stop control and then the fuel; on a cold day, pre-heating; on an electronic engine, any fault warning or inhibit. A blocked air intake or low compression are further possibilities.
questions.reviewNote: S13: the question now asks for a sensible first check and includes the stop control; the explanation covers pre-heating, electronic inhibit, air intake and compression. Please approve.

questions.prompt: Pressing start gives a single click and nothing else. What does this usually point to?
options: A weak battery or a poor connection to the starter
Air in the fuel lines to the injection pump
A raw water strainer blocked with weed
A fuel shut-off valve that was left closed at the tank
questions.explanation: The click is the solenoid trying to engage. Without enough current, the starter cannot turn. Fuel and cooling faults do not stop the engine turning over.

questions.prompt: The engine will not start on a cold morning but starts easily later in the day. Which part is a likely suspect?
options: The glow plugs or their circuit
The stern gland and its packing rings
The raw water pump impeller
The level of the gearbox oil
questions.explanation: Cold starting relies on extra heat from the glow plugs. Once the air is warmer the engine manages without them, which hides the fault.

questions.prompt: Why can long periods of cranking be harmful on an engine with a wet exhaust?
options: Water pumped into the exhaust is not blown out and can flood the cylinders
Unburnt diesel floods the cylinders and washes the oil off the bores
The exhaust gets dangerously hot while the engine is cranking
The raw water pump runs dry while the engine is only cranking
questions.explanation: While cranking, the raw water pump still pushes water into the exhaust, but there is no exhaust gas flow to expel it, so water can build up and reach the cylinders. If repeated cranking fails, stop and follow the engine and exhaust maker's procedure; never run the engine with the seacock closed.

questions.prompt: While cranking, the engine turns a little and then stops hard. What should you do?
options: Stop cranking and get advice, because water may be in the cylinders
Keep cranking, using a freshly charged battery to give more power
Use a starting spray to help it fire before it stops
Bleed the fuel system, then try cranking again straight away
questions.explanation: Water does not compress. If a cylinder is full of it, forcing the engine round, with more cranking or a starting spray, can bend a connecting rod. Do not crank again; get qualified assistance.

questions.prompt: After several attempts, an engine with a wet exhaust still will not start. What should you do?
options: Stop cranking and follow the engine and exhaust maker's procedure
Close the seacock and keep cranking until it fires, then open it
Keep cranking in longer bursts so the exhaust can clear itself
Use a starting spray so it fires before the exhaust fills
questions.explanation: Repeated cranking can let water build up in a wet exhaust and enter the engine. Follow the documented procedure for your installation, and never run the engine with the raw-water seacock closed: an engine that fires with it shut quickly destroys its impeller and exhaust. Longer cranking or a starting spray only adds to the risk, and if water may have got in, do not crank again.
questions.reviewNote: New in content 1.1 (S01, S20): tests the corrected wet-exhaust advice, including the old 'close the seacock' advice as a wrong answer. Please approve.

questions.prompt: The engine slows and fades over several seconds before stopping. What type of cause does this usually point to?
options: A fuel supply problem
A rope round the propeller
A failed glow plug
Low oil pressure
questions.explanation: A gradual fade is typical of fuel starvation, such as a blocked filter or air in the fuel, as the supply dwindles. A rope usually stops the engine abruptly, a glow plug affects only starting, and low oil pressure would set off its alarm.

questions.prompt: The engine runs fine in neutral but stalls as soon as you put it in gear. What is the best response?
options: Stop the engine, make sure it cannot start, then check for something round the propeller
Raise the idle speed with the throttle and keep engaging gear until it holds
Assume the gearbox has failed and call for a tow without checking anything
Engage astern at higher revs to unwind whatever may be caught
questions.explanation: Something round the propeller is one important possibility, but a low idle speed, a gearbox fault or a binding shaft can do the same. Make the engine safe before inspecting near the propeller, and rule things out one at a time. Forcing it in gear or at higher revs can wrap a rope tighter and damage the shaft, gearbox or stern gear.
questions.reviewNote: S12: the question now teaches a safe inspection first instead of naming a single cause. Please approve.

questions.prompt: Over a season, the boat gets slower at the same engine revs and the exhaust smokes black under load. What is a likely cause?
options: A fouled hull or propeller adding load
A worn cutless bearing letting the shaft vibrate
A slipping alternator belt robbing power
Water in the fuel, which burns poorly
questions.explanation: Growth on the hull and propeller adds drag. The engine works harder, burns more fuel than it can use cleanly, and the boat goes slower.

questions.prompt: The engine stops, restarts after a rest, runs for a while and stops again, with no water or dirt in the filter bowl. What might be blocked?
options: The fuel tank vent
The raw water strainer
The oil filter
The exhaust water injection
questions.explanation: With a blocked vent, a vacuum builds in the tank as fuel is used until the lift pump cannot draw any more. Resting lets air leak back in slowly, so the cycle repeats.

questions.prompt: After a rough passage the engine fades over a few seconds and stops. Where should you look first?
options: In the primary fuel filter bowl, for water and dirt
In the coolant header tank, to check the coolant level
At the stern gland, for a faster drip than usual
At the alternator belt, for its tension and wear
questions.explanation: A fading stop points to fuel starvation, and rough water stirs up water and sediment from the bottom of the tank. The primary filter bowl shows quickly whether any has come through.

questions.prompt: Which two warnings mean you should stop the engine as soon as it is safe to do so?
options: Low oil pressure and high temperature
High temperature and the charge warning
Low oil pressure and the glow plug light
The charge warning and low fuel
questions.explanation: Both are stop-engine conditions: reduce power and stop as soon as the boat is safe, and do not restart until the cause is found and corrected. A charge warning needs prompt attention, mainly because the belt may also drive the coolant pump.

questions.prompt: The engine overheated although water was flowing normally from the exhaust. Once it has stopped and cooled, which of these should you check?
options: The drive belt and the coolant level
The raw water seacock
The raw water strainer
Whether the raw water pump has an impeller fitted
questions.explanation: Normal exhaust water shows the raw water side is working. The problem is more likely on the coolant side: a slipping belt, low coolant, the thermostat or a blocked heat exchanger.

questions.prompt: What does blue exhaust smoke usually mean?
options: The engine is burning lubricating oil
The engine has too much fuel for its air
There is unburnt fuel from a cold start
The exhaust is short of cooling water
questions.explanation: Oil burning in the cylinders gives a bluish smoke. Black smoke points to excess fuel, white smoke on a cold start to unburnt fuel, and steam to a cooling problem.

questions.prompt: The charge warning light comes on while motoring. Why should you check the drive belt straight away?
options: If the belt also drives the coolant pump, the engine will soon overheat
Because on most engines the same belt drives the fuel injection pump
Because a broken belt will quickly cause low oil pressure
Because the belt helps keep the propeller shaft in line
questions.explanation: A charge warning indicates a charging-system fault, and on many engines the alternator belt also drives the coolant circulating pump. The warning can therefore be the first sign of an overheating problem to come.

questions.prompt: You suspect a temperature alarm is false because the engine does not feel hot. What is the safe approach?
options: Treat the alarm as real until you have proved otherwise
Disconnect the alarm and carry on
Increase revs to see if it clears
Remove the pressure cap to check the coolant
questions.explanation: Sensors can fail, but so can engines. Ignoring a real warning risks expensive damage, and opening a hot pressure cap risks scalding. Stop, check safely, and get advice if unsure.
